learningObjective: Choose a robust statistic (median or a percentile) rather than mean when reporting kernel latency in the presence of outliers.
stem: Given the following 20 warmed-up per-iter latencies of the same kernel, which single number is the most defensible headline for a report and why?

options.text: The mean (2.98 ms) is a good headline because it summarizes all 20 samples in a single number, and mean is the standard statistic in scientific reporting.
The p99 (12.4 ms) is a good headline because it represents worst-case behavior and captures the tail; when in doubt, always report the worst observed sample as the summary number.
The std (2.5 ms) is the most useful headline because it captures the spread; readers can infer any percentile from mean ± std under the assumption of a normal distribution of kernel latencies.

The median (2.18 ms) is the most defensible headline: it is robust to the two obvious outliers (5.80 ms and 12.4 ms), agrees with the bulk of the distribution, and does not overstate steady-state cost. Ideally the report should include median plus one or more tail percentiles (p95, p99) rather than a single number.

explanation: With 20 samples containing 2 clear outliers, the mean is pulled far above the bulk of the distribution (2.98 vs 2.18 ms). Median (or a robust central estimator like trimmed mean) reflects the typical steady-state behavior; tail percentiles capture the rare bad case. Reporting only mean or only p99 misleads. Standard deviation assumes normality which does not hold for latency (usually right-skewed with a heavy tail).

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: mean is not robust to outliers common in latency distributions.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: p99 on 20 samples is essentially one worst-case sample; unstable and not representative.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: latency distributions are right-skewed; std does not encode percentiles under a normal assumption that fails.
optionExplanations.D: Correct: median (with additional tail percentiles) is the standard robust choice.

assumptions: The two outliers (5.80 ms, 12.4 ms) reflect infrequent noise events (GC, driver events), not the target measurement.
nonImplications: Does not imply mean is never useful; for total-throughput calculations it can be appropriate.
Does not imply p99 should be ignored; it is essential for latency SLOs, just not as a stand-alone headline.

distractorRationales.B: Single-sample p99 with n=20 is unstable.

performanceClaim.scope: Kernel latency reporting statistics under a right-skewed distribution
